# The Infrastructure Underneath Your Agent: What Providers Are Rebuilding and Why It Matters

**Agent Engineering Brief — Video Script**
*As of 16 October 2026*

---

## Description Draft

What happens to your Git repository when agents start making millions of commits? At least two major providers have already rebuilt core development infrastructure to handle agent-scale workloads — and a third has added AI-assisted code review as a shipped feature. This video breaks down what changed, what the evidence actually shows, and what small teams should verify for themselves.

📄 Read the full article: **[ARTICLE LINK — INSERT WHEN PUBLISHED]**
📺 Watch more from Agent Engineering Brief: **[CHANNEL/PLAYLIST LINK — INSERT WHEN PUBLISHED]**

**Sources referenced:**
- GitHub Engineering Blog, "Building Git infrastructure for agent-scale development," 6 Oct 2026 — https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/building-git-infrastructure-for-agent-scale-development/
- Simon Willison, "Redesigning source control at Anthropic," 13 Oct 2026 — https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/13/redesigning-source-control-at-anthropic/
- OpenAI Codex product video, "Code review is no longer the bottleneck," 12 Oct 2026 — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IZXv6a78NDw
- Latent Space podcast, "Claude Code's Next Era — Thariq Shihipar, Anthropic," 29 Sep 2026 — https://www.latent.space/p/thariq

**Disclosure:** This video uses an AI-generated presentation. [SPECIFY TOOL AND VOICE — e.g., "Narration and visuals were produced using HeyGen / Google Vids."] All claims, limitations, and uncertainty are drawn from the underlying evidence brief and are consistent with the accompanying written article. No scenes are presented as real source footage. No quotations are invented.

---

## Visual Style Note for Production

Simple, text-forward slides with minimal animation. Each major section gets a clean header card. Data points appear as large-type callouts. No stock footage of developers meant to imply real events. No simulated demos.

---

## Script

---

**[TITLE CARD: "The Infrastructure Underneath Your Agent"]**
**[SUBTITLE: "Agent Engineering Brief | As of 16 October 2026"]**

---

### SECTION 1 — HOOK

**[VISUAL: Blank dark slide. Single line of text fades in: "7.38 billion commits. One month."]**

> **NARRATION:**
> Here's a number worth pausing on. According to GitHub's own engineering blog, developers and agents made approximately 7.38 billion commits on the platform in September 2026 alone — described by GitHub as more than five times the number from a year earlier. Monthly pushes grew from about 0.69 billion to 3.35 billion over the same period. **[01-c1]**
>
> GitHub attributes much of that growth to agent-driven workloads.
>
> That is not a small shift. And it is forcing providers to rebuild foundational infrastructure that most developers have never had to think about.

**[ON-SCREEN SOURCE CUE: GitHub Engineering Blog, 6 Oct 2026]**

---

### SECTION 2 — THE SCALE PROBLEM

**[VISUAL: Simple diagram — human developer on left, single arrow to repo. Then: many agents, many simultaneous arrows.]**

> **NARRATION:**
> To understand why this matters, consider what happens when an agent commits after nearly every action it takes.
>
> For a human, a push that takes a few seconds is nothing. For an agent in a tight loop, that same latency becomes a ceiling on how fast it can work. Multiply that across thousands of agents operating on a single codebase, and what was once a non-issue becomes a fundamental architectural constraint.
>
> GitHub's current design stores each repository across multiple fileservers for redundancy. That works well at human scale. But the way it achieves redundancy is also the mechanism it uses to serve reads — meaning if you add capacity to handle more read traffic, you also make every write slightly slower. At agent volume, this trade-off stops being acceptable.

**[VISUAL: Simple text card — "Adding read capacity → slower writes. At agent scale, this breaks."]**

---

### SECTION 3 — WHAT GITHUB IS BUILDING

**[VISUAL: Two-column card: "Old Architecture" / "New Architecture" with plain bullet comparisons.]**

> **NARRATION:**
> GitHub's response is a redesign in progress. The core change is to separate durable storage — where repository data actually lives — from the compute layer that answers read requests. Each side can then scale independently. Read spikes from CI pipelines or agent fleets no longer add overhead to writes.
>
> GitHub reports internal benchmarks showing up to 35 times higher write throughput with the new design. **[01-c6]**
>
> That is an impressive figure — but it comes from GitHub's own engineering team, describing work that is not yet complete, tested against their own internal benchmarks, not an independent audit. Treat it as what it is: an attributed claim from a vendor about work in progress.

**[ON-SCREEN SOURCE CUE: GitHub Engineering Blog, 6 Oct 2026 — "internal benchmarks"]**

**[VISUAL: Callout box — "35× write throughput claim | Source: GitHub's own team | Status: In progress | Not independently verified"]**

---

### SECTION 4 — ANTHROPIC'S COMPLETED MIGRATION

**[VISUAL: Simple line chart placeholder — labeled "Daily code merges at Anthropic: May → September 2026." Two data points marked: ~2,500 and ~30,000+.]**

> **NARRATION:**
> Anthropic has reportedly already finished a comparable rebuild. According to Simon Willison, commenting on an Anthropic engineering post — and note, Willison is the intermediary here, not an independent auditor — Anthropic's daily code merges grew from roughly 2,500 in May 2026 to over 30,000 by September. That is approximately a 12-times increase in about four months. **[01-c2]**
>
> In response, the company built a custom source-control system called Scion. It was built by a team of seven people and migrated from Git in five months. Willison notes that Scion has no offline support — a design choice that would be a dealbreaker for human developers, but, as a Scion engineer noted publicly, Claude is by far the heaviest user and is necessarily always online, so offline support was simply not a priority. **[01-c2]**

**[ON-SCREEN SOURCE CUE: Simon Willison, 13 Oct 2026 — summarizing Anthropic engineering post]**

**[VISUAL: Callout — "Scion: no offline support. Claude is the heaviest user. Offline use wasn't the goal."]**

---

### SECTION 5 — OPENAI'S CODE REVIEW FEATURE

**[VISUAL: Clean mockup — not from footage — showing "Agent takes first-pass review → human reads summary → human approves."]**

> **NARRATION:**
> OpenAI's Codex product video, published in mid-October, demonstrates a third example. It shows a code-review workflow where an agent automatically takes a first pass at GitHub pull requests once repository permissions are configured. According to the video, GitHub code review is generally available, with GitLab in preview. **[01-c3]**
>
> What the video does not show: review accuracy, false-positive rates, or how the agent performs on codebases it has not seen before. That gap matters. An automatic first-pass review that flags the wrong things at high volume could add noise faster than it removes it. The video is a product demonstration, not a measurement.

**[ON-SCREEN SOURCE CUE: OpenAI Codex product video, 12 Oct 2026 — demo only; no accuracy data reported]**

---

### SECTION 6 — THE PERMISSION PROBLEM

**[VISUAL: Iceberg diagram — small visible portion labeled "What you granted." Large hidden portion labeled "What the agent could do."]**

> **NARRATION:**
> Underneath all of this infrastructure work is a harder problem: how do you control what agents are actually allowed to do?
>
> A Latent Space podcast published in late September 2026 features an Anthropic employee describing the layers being added to the Claude Code harness — inference-time probes that examine model activations, an "auto mode" that checks whether agent actions match what the user actually granted permission for, and identity isolation for multiplayer contexts where multiple agents operate together. **[01-c4]**
>
> The speaker is an Anthropic employee with clear vendor interest, so these observations reflect internal Anthropic use, not a neutral audit. But what stands out is the candor about what isn't solved yet. The permission and visibility surface area is described as being — quote — like an iceberg. Concrete examples given: an agent in one channel that can message another channel, potentially moving data across permission boundaries it wasn't meant to cross; an agent that could theoretically use computer use to issue its own database credentials in order to complete a task the user never explicitly authorized. **[01-c4]**
>
> These are described as ongoing engineering challenges with known gaps — not as finished, fully secured systems.

**[ON-SCREEN SOURCE CUE: Latent Space podcast, 29 Sep 2026 — Anthropic employee, vendor perspective; transcript paraphrased]**

**[VISUAL: Three-layer stack card: "Inference-time probes | Auto mode permissions check | Identity isolation" — with label: "Described as in progress, not complete"]**

---

### SECTION 7 — WHAT BOTH PROVIDERS ARE EXPLICITLY PROTECTING

**[VISUAL: Simple list card — "Branch protections | Required reviews | Audit logs"]**

> **NARRATION:**
> Here is something both GitHub and Anthropic say explicitly: the new infrastructure must preserve existing governance controls. Branch protections. Required reviews. Audit logs. **[01-c5]**
>
> That framing is actually a signal worth noticing. It suggests both organizations recognize that human-oversight mechanisms are the part of the stack most at risk of being quietly degraded by agent volume — not disabled, just overwhelmed into meaninglessness.
>
> An agent fleet pushing thousands of branches per hour can saturate merge queues and fill review inboxes without anyone turning off a single policy. The infrastructure changes are meant to keep controls functional at scale. But the controls themselves are not being strengthened — they are being defended against a new threat.

**[ON-SCREEN SOURCE CUE: GitHub Engineering Blog, 6 Oct 2026; Simon Willison, 13 Oct 2026]**

---

### SECTION 8 — WHAT THIS MEANS FOR SMALL TEAMS

**[VISUAL: Text card — "Most of this is invisible to you. Here's what isn't."]**

> **NARRATION:**
> Let's be direct about what this evidence does and doesn't mean for a student developer or a small team.
>
> The infrastructure rebuilds described here are almost entirely relevant to large organizations running agent fleets at scale. Most individual developers interact with GitHub through standard clients and will not see or configure anything in the new architecture.
>
> Whether the Codex code-review feature changes your daily workflow depends on whether you use that product and whether the automated review quality is actually good enough to be worth reading. That is something you would need to test yourself — it has not been independently measured.
>
> None of the sources in this assessment represent the experience of small teams, students, or unsuccessful deployments. That is a real gap in the evidence, not a minor caveat.

**[VISUAL: Callout box — "Missing voices in this evidence: small teams, students, unsuccessful deployments."]**

---

### SECTION 9 — THE QUESTION TO KEEP

**[VISUAL: Single question on screen: "When agents fill your review queue — what does your review practice actually become?"]**

> **NARRATION:**
> If platforms are already designing source control around agents as the primary users — with human offline support explicitly deprioritized — then the practical question for any team enabling coding agents is not whether to turn them on.
>
> It is this: which of your existing controls are you going to verify are still working once you do?
>
> Branch protections and required reviews are only meaningful if a human actually reads the diff before approving. An automatic first-pass review is only useful if someone checks whether the first pass is accurate. The infrastructure providers are trying to preserve the conditions for human oversight. Whether human oversight actually happens is still up to your team.

---

### CLOSING

**[VISUAL: Title card with publication name and as-of date]**

> **NARRATION:**
> This is Agent Engineering Brief. The accompanying article goes deeper on each of these claims, with source links and explicit notes on what is a verified fact, what is an attributed vendor claim, and what is inference. Link in the description.
>
> These are real changes at real scale. Most of them are not yours to configure. But the governance question they raise — that one is yours to answer.

**[VISUAL: Source summary card]**

**[ON-SCREEN: GitHub Engineering Blog, 6 Oct 2026 | Simon Willison, 13 Oct 2026 | OpenAI Codex video, 12 Oct 2026 | Latent Space podcast, 29 Sep 2026]**

**[VISUAL: Disclosure card — "AI-generated presentation. [SPECIFY TOOL]. Claims consistent with underlying evidence brief. No real footage simulated. No quotations invented."]**
